notes: Yang Jian founded the Sui dynasty in 581, conquered the Chen dynasty in 589, and reunified China. He reigned until 604.
Sun Quan proclaimed himself emperor of Eastern Wu in 229 after ruling as King of Wu and reigned until his death in 252.
Zheng He led seven major treasure voyages between 1405 and 1433 under the Yongle and Xuande emperors, extending Ming diplomatic and maritime influence across the Indian Ocean.
Li Zicheng founded the Shun dynasty, captured Beijing in 1644, and ruled until the collapse of his regime in 1645.
Zhang Xianzhong founded the Great Western Kingdom in Sichuan in 1644 and ruled until his death in 1647.
Yuan Shao was a major late Eastern Han warlord who led the coalition against Dong Zhuo and controlled much of northern China until his death in 202.
Wu Zetian founded the Wu Zhou dynasty in 690 and ruled as emperor until her abdication in 705.
Zhang Jue founded the Taiping Dao movement and led the Yellow Turban Rebellion against the Eastern Han in 184.
The Kangxi Emperor reigned from 1661 to 1722, consolidated Qing rule, suppressed the Revolt of the Three Feudatories, and incorporated Taiwan into the empire.
Chen Youliang founded the Chen Han regime and proclaimed himself emperor in 1360. He died during the Battle of Lake Poyang in 1363.
Zhang Shicheng established the Great Zhou regime and ruled much of the lower Yangtze region from Suzhou until his defeat in 1367.
Fang Guozhen was a maritime warlord who controlled the Zhejiang coast during the late Yuan and ultimately surrendered to Zhu Yuanzhang in 1367.
Ming Yuzhen founded the Ming Xia regime in Sichuan, proclaimed himself emperor in 1362, and ruled until his death in 1366.
Liu Futong was a principal leader of the Red Turban Rebellion and the leading military figure of the restored Song regime until his death in 1363.
Toghon Temur reigned as emperor of the Yuan dynasty from 1333 until the Ming capture of Dadu in 1368.
After retreating from Dadu in 1368, Toghon Temur continued to rule the Northern Yuan until his death in 1370.
Koke Temur served as a leading late Yuan general against rebel and Ming forces until the fall of Dadu in 1368.
Koke Temur remained one of the principal military commanders of the Northern Yuan from 1368 until his death in 1375.
Bolad Temur was a powerful late Yuan warlord based in Datong who occupied Dadu in 1364 and dominated the court until his assassination in 1365.
King Zhuang of Chu reigned from 613 to 591 BCE and made Chu the dominant power of the Spring and Autumn period.
The Yongzheng Emperor reigned from 1722 to 1735 and strengthened central authority and fiscal administration.
Hong Xiuquan founded the Taiping Heavenly Kingdom in 1851 and ruled as Heavenly King until his death in 1864.
Ching Shih commanded the Red Flag Fleet from 1807 until accepting amnesty from the Qing government in 1810.
Zhu Yuanzhang founded the Ming dynasty in 1368 and ruled until his death in 1398.
Li Longji reigned as Emperor Xuanzong of Tang from 712 to 756. His early reign marked the Kaiyuan prosperity, while his later years culminated in the An Lushan Rebellion.

Xiang Yu established Western Chu after the fall of the Qin dynasty and ruled as Hegemon-King from 206 to 202 BCE. He was Liu Bang's principal rival during the Chu-Han Contention and was defeated at Gaixia in 202 BCE.
Dong Zhuo seized control of the Eastern Han court in 189, deposed Emperor Shao, installed Emperor Xian, and ruled as the de facto head of the imperial government until his assassination in 192.
Yuan Shu proclaimed himself emperor of the Zhong dynasty in 197. His regime rapidly declined and collapsed before his death in 199.
Liu Biao governed Jing Province as one of the most powerful regional warlords of the late Eastern Han from 190 until his death in 208.
Xiaobai, posthumously known as Duke Huan of Qi, ruled Qi from 685 to 643 BCE and became the first of the Five Hegemons with the assistance of Guan Zhong.
Zifu, posthumously known as Duke Xiang of Song, ruled Song from 650 to 637 BCE and pursued hegemony during the Spring and Autumn period.
Chonger, posthumously known as Duke Wen of Jin, returned from exile to rule Jin from 636 to 628 BCE and became one of the Five Hegemons.
Renhao, posthumously known as Duke Mu of Qin, ruled Qin from 659 to 621 BCE and expanded Qin's power across western China.
Helu ruled Wu from 514 to 496 BCE and transformed it into a major power with the assistance of Wu Zixu and Sun Tzu.
Goujian ruled Yue from 496 to 465 BCE, rebuilt the state after defeat by Wu, conquered Wu in 473 BCE, and became a hegemon of the late Spring and Autumn period.
Ji Wusheng, posthumously known as Duke Zhuang of Zheng, ruled Zheng from 743 to 701 BCE and made it the leading power of the early Spring and Autumn period.
Ying Bu, also known as Qing Bu, was enfeoffed as King of Huainan by Liu Bang after supporting Han during the Chu-Han Contention. He ruled from 202 to 196 BCE before rebelling and being defeated.
Wang Mang usurped the Western Han throne and founded the Xin dynasty in 9 CE. His reforms failed amid widespread unrest, and he was killed during the collapse of the dynasty in 23 CE.
Tian Heng was the last independent leader of the restored State of Qi during the Chu-Han Contention and died in 202 BCE after refusing to submit to Han rule.
Zhang Han was a leading Qin general who surrendered to Xiang Yu and was enfeoffed as King of Yong. He ruled until his defeat by Liu Bang in 205 BCE.
Liu Bingyi, later renamed Liu Xun and posthumously known as Emperor Xuan of Han, reigned from 74 to 49 BCE and restored the strength of the Western Han.
Zhao Tuo founded Nanyue around 204 BCE following the collapse of Qin and ruled until 137 BCE over a kingdom spanning Lingnan and northern Vietnam.
Liu Xiu founded the Eastern Han dynasty in 25 CE, reunified much of China, and restored Han imperial rule.
Liu Yu founded the Liu Song dynasty in 420 after overthrowing the Eastern Jin and ruled until 422.
Huang Chao proclaimed himself emperor of Great Qi after capturing Chang'an in 881. His regime collapsed in 884.
Zhu Wen overthrew the Tang dynasty and founded the Later Liang in 907, beginning the Five Dynasties period. He ruled until 912.
Li Keyong was a Shatuo military leader and Prince of Jin who established the political and military foundation from which his son founded the Later Tang dynasty.
Li Cunxu founded the Later Tang dynasty in 923, defeated the Later Liang, and ruled until his death during a mutiny in 926.
Li Siyuan reigned as Emperor Mingzong of Later Tang from 926 to 933 and restored political stability after the death of Emperor Zhuangzong.
Shi Jingtang founded the Later Jin dynasty in 936 with Khitan support and ceded the Sixteen Prefectures to the Liao. He ruled until 942.
Liu Zhiyuan founded the Later Han dynasty in 947 after the collapse of the Later Jin and ruled until his death in 948.
Guo Wei overthrew the Later Han and founded the Later Zhou dynasty in 951. His reforms were continued by his successor.
Guo Rong reigned as Emperor Shizong of Later Zhou from 954 to 959 and strengthened the state through military victories and administrative reforms.
Ying Quliang, posthumously known as Duke Xiao of Qin, ruled Qin from 361 to 338 BCE and sponsored Shang Yang's reforms.
Ying Ji, posthumously known as King Zhaoxiang of Qin, ruled from 306 to 251 BCE and made Qin the dominant Warring States power.
Tian Yinqi, posthumously known as King Wei of Qi, ruled from 356 to 320 BCE and transformed Qi into one of the strongest Warring States powers.
Xiong Shang, posthumously known as King Wei of Chu, reigned from 339 to 329 BCE during the height of Chu's power.
Ji Zhi, posthumously known as King Zhao of Yan, reigned from 311 to 279 BCE and rebuilt Yan after the Qi invasion.
Zhao Yong, posthumously known as King Wuling of Zhao, ruled from 325 to 299 BCE and introduced the Hu clothing and cavalry reforms.
Wei Ying, posthumously known as King Hui of Wei, ruled from 370 to 319 BCE and moved the capital to Daliang.
Han Qu, posthumously known as Marquess Lie of Han and also recorded as Marquess Wu of Han, ruled from 399 to 387 BCE.
Zhao Xu reigned as Emperor Shenzong of Song from 1067 to 1085 and supported Wang Anshi's New Policies.
Weiming Yuanhao, also known as Li Yuanhao, founded the Western Xia Empire in 1038 and ruled until 1048.
Nurhaci founded the Later Jin in 1616 after unifying the Jurchen tribes and established the Eight Banners system.
